I’ve worked this land for 40 years, and at 72, I know exactly what my 1.2 mu can do and what my back can handle. I live alone, so I don’t take risks or try fancy new methods—I stick to the wheat-maize double crop that has always put food on my table. My well gives me reliable water when the sky doesn’t, which is why I can keep this rotation going. For winter wheat, I’ll rotary-till the field after the maize comes off, then sow improved seed in autumn with a base dressing of compound fertilizer. I’ll top-dress with urea at the jointing stage, irrigate three times—before winter dormancy, at jointing, and during grain filling—and spray twice for weeds and leaf rust. In early June, the moment the wheat is harvested, I’ll sow hybrid maize with no-tillage; at my age, there’s no time or strength to plough in that summer heat, and the no-till seeder works fine. I’ll fertilize at sowing and again at the big trumpet stage, irrigate twice when the ears are forming and filling, and spray twice to control weeds and corn borers. It is a modest plan, but it is honest work that one old man can finish.
